title: Rich or Wealthy? There's a Difference
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Looking rich and being wealthy are not the same thing. Why luxury display often masks debt, and what a wealthy mindset actually looks like.
content: Rich or Wealthy? There's a Difference By Vanessa Stoykov There is a phenomenon on social media at the moment in China called 'flaunt your wealth'. The idea is people lying next to their luxury car as if they have fallen out, with their personal belongings from their bag spread around them. These items are luxury products that prove how much they have to spend. Their hashtag on Instagram is #fallingstars It occurred to me when reading about this in the press that this is a prime example of people who want to show that they are rich. But the bigger question is — are they wealthy? In today's world of brands and relatively easy access to credit, it has not been too hard for people to look like they are rich. European cars, clothes with high end labels all over them, and jewellery and handbags to give the display of money. Looking rich is not the same as owning anything What has not always gone with this display is real wealth. While rich may be all the luxury items that are displayed to the world, a lot of the time those people have no real assets that they own, and no liquidity or cash if they needed it. Many are living from one pay cycle to the next while paying off all the beautiful things they own — which instantly lose value and keep them in a cycle of debt. While the #fallingstars might be the extreme of these examples, the difference between rich and wealthy is obvious at home too. It's why as a nation we are in a massive amount of personal debt, and mortgages are so high. While many of us aspire to the finer things in life, much of the time we can't really afford them. So what starts as 'treat yourself to the best' becomes a life trapped in an endless cycle of paying for what you never could really afford. What wealthy actually looks like Wealthy people have multiple income streams, lots of assets they own and they keep their overheads as low as possible to maintain a standard of living that is comfortable but not wasteful. title: Should You Be a Guarantor for Your Adult Child's Home Loan?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Before you guarantee your adult child's home loan, understand the real risks to your retirement and how to protect yourself.
content: ← Back to Adult Children ARTICLE Should You Be a Guarantor for Your Adult Child's Home Loan? By Vanessa Stoykov When an adult child asks you to guarantee their first home loan, you're not just facing a paperwork decision, you're staring down one of the biggest money conversations in modern family life. As property prices soar and lending criteria tighten in Australia, the pressure on parents to help out is real. But before you sign anything, it's crucial to understand exactly what you're taking on; and how it could impact your own retirement planning. Understand the Real Risks of Being a Guarantor Agreeing to be a guarantor for your child's mortgage isn't just a kind gesture, it's a binding financial commitment. If your child can't meet their repayments, the bank can demand the guaranteed amount from you. This could put your own home or retirement savings at risk, especially if you're close to retiring and have fewer years to recover financially. You might trust your child completely, but life is unpredictable. Job loss, illness, relationship breakdown, or rising interest rates can happen to anyone. If disaster strikes, being a guarantor can quickly turn from supportive to stressful. Ask the Right Questions Before You Decide It's normal to feel torn between wanting to help your child and needing to protect your own future. Start by having a frank, honest conversation as a family. Ask questions like: What happens if your income changes or you lose your job? How long do you realistically expect the guarantee to stay in place? What is the plan for refinancing down the track? Could buying a less expensive property remove the need for a guarantor? Having these conversations early helps set clear expectations and avoids future conflict. Protecting your own retirement is not selfish, it's smart. title: Supporting Adult Children Financially: Fairness, Boundaries and Your Future
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Helped one child buy a home and now the others expect the same? How to navigate fairness without sacrificing your own security.
content: ← Back to Adult Children ARTICLE Supporting Adult Children Financially: Fairness, Boundaries and Your Future By Vanessa Stoykov It's a dilemma facing thousands of parents across Australia: you've helped one child buy a home, and now your other children are expecting the same. With property prices surging, supporting adult children financially feels almost obligatory. But what happens when your desire to be 'fair' risks your own financial wellbeing? If you're weighing up whether to dip into savings or super to help your children, you're not alone. Many in their 50s and 60s quietly sacrifice their own retirement plans out of guilt, love, or a sense of obligation. Before you act, here's what you need to consider to avoid the most common mistakes. 1. Sacrificing Your Own Security for Fairness It's natural to want to treat children equally. But fairness doesn't always mean identical outcomes, especially when your financial circumstances have changed. Many parents drain their nest egg to help multiple children, only to realise too late that their own retirement is now under threat. You may be living another 30–40 years, don't give away money you might need for your own security. REAL-LIFE EXAMPLE Margaret, 59, used her savings to help her eldest daughter buy a unit. Two years later, her youngest asked for the same support, but Margaret's financial situation had changed. She felt torn, wanting to be fair, but afraid she'd run out of money. The stress impacted her sleep and health, and family dinners became tense. Ultimately, Margaret realised she could not help both without risking her own future. How to avoid this mistake: Be honest about your current financial situation, don't promise what you can't afford. Model your retirement needs using tools like the MoneySmart Retirement Planner. title: Supporting Adult Children Financially: How to Protect Their Future
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Helped your adult child buy property and worried about a new relationship in the mix? How to protect what you've built.
content: ← Back to Adult Children ARTICLE Supporting Adult Children Financially: How to Protect Their Future By Vanessa Stoykov Helping your adult child get onto the property ladder is a proud moment; but it can be stressful when a new relationship enters the mix. Financial planning after 50 often means balancing your desire to support your children with the need to protect what you've worked hard to build. If you're worried about your child's financial security and the future of a property you helped them buy, you're not alone. Here's what you need to know about safeguarding financial gifts and starting courageous conversations around money and relationships. Understand What Happens When You Give Financial Support When you give your child money for a deposit or major purchase, it usually becomes their legal asset, especially if you haven't set up a formal loan or agreement. This is common in Australia and many other countries. Once given, the money and resulting asset are in your child's name and under their control. That can be a tough pill to swallow, especially if you see them making big life decisions quickly, like moving in with a new partner or talking about marriage. It's normal to feel protective. But your ability to influence the outcome is now about information, not control. Trying to force the issue often backfires, as many parents have seen. Encourage Education, Not Interrogation Raising questions about protecting assets can easily feel like criticism to a child in a new relationship. Instead, frame your concerns as a desire to help them understand their options. For example, suggest they talk to a lawyer about what happens if a partner moves in or if they get married. This helps shift the conversation from emotion to practical facts. title: Supporting Adult Children Financially: Where to Draw the Line as a Parent
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: When does supporting adult children financially cross into enabling? Five warning signs and a healthier way to set boundaries.
content: ← Back to Adult Children ARTICLE Supporting Adult Children Financially: Where to Draw the Line as a Parent By Vanessa Stoykov If you've spent years helping your children get ahead, covering school fees, university costs, or even contributing to their first home deposit, you're not alone. In Australia, more parents are finding that support for adult children doesn't always end at 18 or even 25. But when does helping cross the line into enabling, and how can you protect your own financial wellbeing? It's a tricky balancing act. Many parents feel stuck between guilt and resentment, especially when their partner doesn't share the same boundaries. If you want to avoid common traps and protect both your relationships and your financial future, read on. Here are five critical mistakes to avoid when supporting adult children financially: 1. Not Setting Clear Boundaries One of the biggest mistakes is allowing financial support to continue without clear limits. Without boundaries, expectations can spiral, leaving you feeling drained and underappreciated. Parents often fall into this trap out of love, but it can create dependence rather than empowerment. REAL-LIFE EXAMPLE Karen, 56, always wanted her son to have what she didn't. She paid for every extracurricular activity, university fees, and even helped with his first car. Now at 29, he still asks for help with rent and bills. Karen feels torn between wanting to help and resenting the constant requests. How to avoid this mistake: Communicate your limits clearly, decide what you can give, and for how long. Have an honest conversation with your partner about what support looks like now. Stick to agreed boundaries to avoid confusion and resentment. 2. Giving Money Without Partner Agreement When one parent gives money in secret, it creates mistrust and mixed messages. This can fracture your relationship and make you feel like the 'bad guy.' Consistency between parents is vital for healthy family dynamics and financial security.

title: Aged Care Planning: Avoid These 3 Costly Mistakes in Your Family
author: Conrad Francis
excerpt: Most families are caught off guard by aged care timing, not cost. Three mistakes to avoid before the late-night phone call comes.
content: ← Back to Ageing Parents ARTICLE Aged Care Planning: Avoid These 3 Costly Mistakes in Your Family By Conrad Francis If you're like many Australians over 50, the idea of a late-night phone call about a parent's health is a scenario you secretly dread. When it comes to aged care planning, most families get caught off guard, not by paperwork or costs, but by the timing. Retirement planning in Australia isn't just about super or pensions; it's about conversations nobody wants to have, until it's almost too late. Why does this happen? Because talking openly about aged care feels confronting. Many people put off the conversation, hoping to respect a parent's independence or simply not knowing how to start. But here's the truth: avoiding these discussions is one of the biggest mistakes you can make. Here are three critical mistakes to avoid when planning aged care for your family. 1. Waiting Until Crisis Hits Too many families wait until a parent has a fall, a hospital stay, or a sudden decline before talking about aged care. By then, decisions must be made fast, often under pressure, and with incomplete information. When time isn't on your side, small disagreements can become major family rifts. REAL-LIFE EXAMPLE Lisa, 56, always assumed there would be time to talk to her mum about moving somewhere safer “one day.” When her mum fell and couldn’t return home, Lisa and her siblings had just 72 hours to agree on a care facility, with no idea what their mother really wanted. The stress and guilt lingered for years. How to avoid this mistake: Find your “quiet Sunday.” Bring up the topic before a crisis makes it urgent. Ask open questions early. “Would you want to stay at home, or move somewhere with support if you needed more help?” Document preferences. Write down what matters most to your parent and share with all siblings. 2. title: Do You Actually Know What Your Parents Own — and Owe?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Why families often discover financial complexity too late and how to discuss assets, debts and documents without taking over.
content: ← Back to Ageing Parents ARTICLE Do You Actually Know What Your Parents Own — and Owe? By Vanessa Stoykov Adult children often assume their parents' finances are simple. There is a home, a pension or retirement income, perhaps some savings. Then a health event reveals an old loan, unpaid bills, a guarantee for someone else, scattered accounts or paperwork nobody can find — and the "simple" picture turns out to have been an assumption rather than a fact. The problem is not that children failed to investigate. Parents are entitled to privacy. The problem is that a family can mistake privacy for preparedness, only discovering the difference when it's least convenient to sort out. Ask about the map, not every number A respectful first step is to ask whether your parents have a current list of their important assets, debts, policies and advisers, and where it is stored. They may prefer not to share balances while they are well, and that preference should be respected. What matters is that someone trusted can locate information if needed and that legal authorities are properly arranged. A password scribbled in a drawer is not a complete plan, however well-intentioned it was at the time. IN PRACTICE When her father was hospitalised unexpectedly, one woman spent an entire afternoon on the phone trying to identify which bank held his savings, because the only clue was a faded statement in a drawer with no account number visible. It took nearly two weeks and several trips to different branches to build a complete picture of his finances — time that could have been spent on far more important things, if a simple list had existed beforehand. Look for complexity Common complications include jointly owned property, family loans, business interests, guarantees, overseas assets, digital accounts, former relationships and outdated beneficiaries. title: Inheritance Isn't a Financial Plan
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Why relying on a future inheritance can distort your finances, career and family relationships — and what to do instead.
content: ← Back to Ageing Parents ARTICLE Inheritance Isn't a Financial Plan By Vanessa Stoykov Many adults quietly include an inheritance in their future. They may save less, delay dealing with debt or assume a parent's home will eventually solve retirement. Nobody has necessarily promised anything, but the expectation becomes part of the plan almost by default, simply because it's easier than confronting the alternative. That is risky financially and emotionally. Parents may live longer, need expensive care, change their will, remarry, support another family member or simply choose to spend their own money — any of which can quietly dismantle a plan that was never actually agreed to in the first place. Your parents' money belongs to them A parent's assets are not a family reserve waiting to be distributed. They are resources for that person's housing, health, care, enjoyment and choices, for as long as they are alive to use them. Holding this truth can be difficult when adult children are under pressure. But expecting access can turn concern about a parent's spending into surveillance and make every family decision feel like a threat to a future entitlement nobody actually promised. IN PRACTICE A man in his fifties had quietly structured much of his own retirement planning around the assumption he'd inherit his parents' home, which was mortgage-free and, in his mind, effectively "his" already. When his mother, widowed and in her eighties, decided to sell it and move into a retirement village that used most of the proceeds, he was genuinely shocked — not because she'd done anything wrong, but because he'd never actually asked her intentions and had simply built years of assumptions on top of silence. Plan from what you control Build decisions around your income, savings, debt and realistic retirement position. title: The Conversation You Need to Have With Your Parents Before There's a Crisis
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How to begin respectful conversations with ageing parents about money, care, housing, wishes and important documents.
content: ← Back to Ageing Parents ARTICLE The Conversation You Need to Have With Your Parents Before There's a Crisis By Vanessa Stoykov Families can discuss holidays, grandchildren and politics, yet avoid the questions that will eventually affect everyone: What do Mum and Dad want if they need care? Can they afford it? Where are the important documents? Who can make decisions if they cannot? These are rarely the questions anyone wants to raise over Sunday lunch. Avoidance often comes from love. Adult children do not want to seem intrusive, and parents do not want to feel old or managed. But silence does not preserve independence. It can leave a family making urgent decisions without knowing the person's wishes, at precisely the moment those wishes matter most. Begin with care, not control Choose a calm moment and explain why you are asking. You might say, 'I want to understand what matters to you so we can support your choices if something changes.' Do not open by demanding account balances — the tone of the first conversation sets the tone for every one that follows. Parents have the right to privacy and to make their own decisions while they have capacity. Your role is to invite a conversation, listen and identify gaps — not to take over decisions that are still genuinely theirs to make. IN PRACTICE One family only discovered their father's wishes about aged care after a fall put him in hospital and a decision had to be made within days. His three adult children each assumed something different about what he'd want, and the disagreement that followed added real strain to an already frightening week. His daughter later said the hardest part wasn't the decision itself — it was realising they'd never actually asked him, in over sixty years, what he'd want in that exact situation. Cover wishes and practical information Discuss preferred living arrangements, care, medical decision-making, wills, powers of attorney or local equivalents, funeral wishes and the people they trust.

title: When You Become the Parent to Your Parents
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: The emotional and financial reality of supporting ageing parents while managing work, children and your own future.
content: ← Back to Ageing Parents ARTICLE When You Become the Parent to Your Parents By Vanessa Stoykov It may begin with a lift to an appointment or help paying a bill online. Then come regular calls, medication, repairs, forms, care decisions and worries in the middle of the night. Without anyone deciding it, you have become the organiser of your parents' lives, one small task quietly becoming a permanent role. Many people reach this point while still working, supporting children and trying to prepare for their own retirement. The practical load is large, but the emotional shift can be even harder — the sense that the direction of care in the relationship has quietly reversed. Care work is real work Family care is often invisible because it happens in small pieces. Track the hours, travel and expenses for a month. Seeing the load clearly can make it easier to ask siblings for specific help and to discuss workplace flexibility with something concrete rather than a general sense of being overwhelmed. Do not wait until exhaustion makes every conversation sound like an accusation. 'I need you to take Mum to two appointments each month' is more useful than 'I do everything,' even when it feels like the truer sentence in the moment. IN PRACTICE A woman juggling a full-time job, two teenagers and her mother's increasing needs kept a simple diary for a month, almost as an experiment. She was startled to find she'd spent eleven hours on appointments, calls and paperwork that month alone — time she'd never consciously registered as "work" because it happened in fragments between everything else. Showing that diary to her brother, rather than simply telling him she needed help, was what finally got him to take over the monthly pharmacy run. Protect your own financial future Adult children may reduce work, cover household bills or use savings to keep a parent at home. title: Who Pays for Mum and Dad? When Siblings Don't Agree
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How siblings can address unequal money, time and caring contributions for ageing parents before resentment damages the family.
content: ← Back to Ageing Parents ARTICLE Who Pays for Mum and Dad? When Siblings Don't Agree By Vanessa Stoykov In many families, one sibling lives closer, answers every call and knows the names of the doctors. Another contributes money. A third is busy or absent. Everyone may love their parents, but the work and cost are rarely distributed evenly, and almost nobody sits down early enough to actually discuss that imbalance out loud. Resentment grows when these differences remain unspoken. The hands-on sibling feels abandoned. The financial contributor feels their help is overlooked. Parents may avoid asking for anything because they fear causing conflict between children they love equally. Name the full contribution Create a shared picture of what support involves: appointments, meals, administration, home maintenance, emotional support, travel and money. Time has value even when nobody sends an invoice for it. Do not assume equality means identical tasks. A sibling overseas may contribute differently from the person nearby. The aim is a transparent arrangement that feels workable, not a perfectly symmetrical roster that nobody can actually maintain. IN PRACTICE Three brothers had quietly resented each other for years over their father's care — the eldest felt like the only one who showed up, while the youngest, who lived interstate, felt his monthly financial contribution went unacknowledged every time it came up. It wasn't until a family meeting, prompted by their father's declining health, that they actually listed out everything each of them contributed. The eldest was startled to learn how much his brother had quietly been paying towards their father's home care — money he'd never mentioned because he assumed it "didn't count" compared to being physically present. Separate the parents' money from the children's Understand the parents' resources and entitlements before siblings begin paying informally. title: The Hidden Financial Cost of Staying in a Job You Hate
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How staying in the wrong job can affect health, confidence, earnings and future opportunities — and how to plan a safer change.
content: ← Back to Career & Income ARTICLE The Hidden Financial Cost of Staying in a Job You Hate By Vanessa Stoykov Leaving a job has visible costs: lost income, uncertainty and perhaps a gap before the next role. Staying has costs too, but they are easier to ignore because they arrive slowly, disguised as ordinary tiredness rather than a genuine financial drain. You may spend more to recover from work, stop investing in skills, turn down opportunities because you have no energy or remain underpaid because your confidence has shrunk along with everything else. Calculate the stay cost Look at direct spending connected to stress and convenience, but also at lost growth. Has your salary stalled? Are your skills becoming less current? Have you stopped building relationships outside the organisation that once opened doors for you? Consider the impact on health and family life. Not every difficult season requires resignation, but chronic damage deserves to be counted honestly rather than dismissed as "just part of the job." It also helps to separate a genuinely difficult period from a genuinely wrong fit. Every role has stretches that are demanding, boring or frustrating — that alone is not evidence you are in the wrong place. The distinction usually shows up in recovery time. A hard month you can bounce back from is different from a role that leaves you depleted no matter how much rest you get around it. IN PRACTICE A woman in a toxic sales role tallied, almost as an exercise, what the job had actually cost her over eighteen months — takeaway meals because she was too exhausted to cook, a gym membership she'd stopped using, and a course she'd abandoned halfway through because she had no energy left after work. The total surprised her more than her actual salary did. Seeing the real cost of "staying" in black and white was what finally pushed her to start job hunting in earnest. title: The Pay Rise Conversation Most Women Put Off for Too Long
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How to prepare for a pay rise conversation using evidence, timing and a clear request — without apologising for asking.
content: ← Back to Career & Income ARTICLE The Pay Rise Conversation Most Women Put Off for Too Long By Vanessa Stoykov Many women work on the assumption that excellent performance will eventually speak for itself. They take on more, solve problems quietly and wait for someone senior to recognise the gap between their contribution and pay. It is a reasonable-sounding strategy that, in practice, rarely delivers what it promises. Sometimes recognition comes. Often it does not. Organisations respond to budgets, timing, internal comparisons and clear requests — not only merit, and certainly not to silent hope that someone else will notice. Prepare an evidence case Document outcomes, not effort. What improved because of your work? Include revenue, savings, delivery, client feedback, risk managed, people developed and responsibilities added since your role or pay was last reviewed. Research an appropriate range using credible market information and comparable roles. Decide on the specific salary, adjustment or review process you will request, rather than leaving the number vague and hoping the other side lands somewhere generous. It is worth asking, too, whether your organisation's normal review cycle is actually working in your favour. Some workplaces default to modest annual increments regardless of the value someone has added, which quietly rewards patience over performance. If your case is strong, there is nothing wrong with requesting a conversation outside the usual cycle rather than waiting for a date the calendar happens to set. IN PRACTICE A finance professional had absorbed the responsibilities of a more senior colleague who left, without any change to her title or pay, assuming the promotion would follow naturally once management noticed. title: What If the Career You Built Isn't the Career You Want Anymore?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How to change career direction in midlife without dismissing your experience or creating unnecessary financial risk.
content: ← Back to Career & Income ARTICLE What If the Career You Built Isn't the Career You Want Anymore? By Vanessa Stoykov You can be successful at work and still know it no longer fits. The title may be good, the income important and other people impressed. Yet Monday arrives with a heaviness that rest never quite fixes, no matter how many weekends you give it to recover. In midlife, changing direction can feel indulgent because the stakes are real: mortgages, children, retirement savings and a reputation built over decades. The choice is not always stay or blow everything up, though it can feel that binary from the inside. Identify what you actually want to leave Is the problem the work, the workplace, the hours, the leadership, the industry or the role you have grown into? A new employer may solve a culture problem. A redesigned role may solve an energy problem — and these require very different responses. Be specific before sacrificing income and certainty. Escaping a feeling without understanding it can lead you to reproduce the same situation somewhere else, just with a different logo on the building. A useful test is to imagine the exact same role, at the exact same seniority, inside a workplace you actually admired. Does the thought still feel heavy? If the heaviness lifts, the problem was likely the environment, not the work itself. If it does not lift, the discontent probably sits closer to the role or the industry, and a change of employer alone is unlikely to solve it. IN PRACTICE A senior operations executive assumed for years that leaving corporate life entirely was the only fix for his exhaustion, until a coach asked him to break down exactly what drained him. It turned out the industry and the work itself still interested him deeply — what had worn him down was eighteen months under one particular leader. A internal transfer to a different division, under different management, resolved almost everything he'd been planning to escape by quitting altogether.

title: You're Not Too Old to Earn More Money
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Why your 40s and 50s can be a powerful time to increase income by using experience, confidence and relationships differently.
content: ← Back to Career & Income ARTICLE You're Not Too Old to Earn More Money By Vanessa Stoykov There is a quiet story many people absorb in their 40s and 50s: the big career moves are behind you, younger people are coming through and you should be grateful simply to stay employed. It can make capable people lower their expectations just when their experience is at its strongest and most sellable. Ageism is real, and career change is not effortless. But experience, judgement, relationships and the ability to solve complex human problems also have economic value. The challenge is to make that value visible to the people deciding what to pay for it. Stop describing yourself by your job title A title tells people where you sit. It does not explain the outcomes you create. Identify the problems you solve, the decisions you improve and the trust you have built. Those capabilities can travel across roles and industries far more easily than the title itself. Keep a record of results: revenue influenced, costs avoided, teams developed, clients retained and projects delivered. Evidence makes a stronger case than years served, and most people underestimate how much evidence they actually have sitting unrecorded. IN PRACTICE A marketing manager in her late 40s had spent fifteen years assuming her career had plateaued, watching younger colleagues get promoted around her. When a mentor suggested she actually list, in writing, every campaign she'd led and its measurable result, she was startled to discover she'd generated several million dollars in attributable revenue over her career — numbers she had simply never bothered to track because she'd been too busy doing the work. That single document became the basis of a pitch for a senior role she'd assumed was out of reach. Increase value before chasing volume Earning more does not always mean working more hours. title: Your Income Is Your Biggest Financial Asset. Are You Investing in It?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Why skills, relationships, reputation and confidence deserve the same attention as savings and investments.
content: ← Back to Career & Income ARTICLE Your Income Is Your Biggest Financial Asset. Are You Investing in It? By Vanessa Stoykov We often talk about building wealth as if it begins only after money reaches an investment account. But the source of most contributions, repayments and choices is income. Your capacity to keep earning is a major financial asset — arguably the largest one most people will ever hold. Unlike a bank balance, that asset is not shown neatly on a statement. It lives in skills, health, reputation, relationships, judgement and the demand for what you can do, which makes it easy to neglect precisely because it's invisible. Maintain the asset Ask whether your skills are becoming more valuable or simply more familiar. What has changed in your industry? Which tasks are becoming automated? Which human capabilities — trust, leadership, sales, creativity or complex judgement — are becoming more important as a result? Choose development connected to a real opportunity, not learning for its own sake. A useful skill should improve the problems you can solve and the evidence you can show for having solved them. IN PRACTICE An accountant who had done the same style of work for over a decade noticed junior colleagues increasingly handling the routine compliance tasks that had once been his bread and butter, faster and more cheaply than he could. Rather than assuming this was simply "how things were now," he invested a year into building advisory skills the automated tools couldn't replicate — the kind of judgement-based client conversations software still can't have. Within two years, his role had shifted entirely towards the higher-value work, and his income had grown alongside it. title: Divorce and Financial Planning: Critical Lessons For Women After 50
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Divorce after 50 can change your life overnight. Critical financial lessons every woman navigating separation should know.
content: ← Back to Divorce ARTICLE Divorce and Financial Planning: Critical Lessons For Women After 50 By Vanessa Stoykov Divorce after 50 isn't just an emotional journey, it's a financial flashpoint that can change your life overnight. Many women who have worked tirelessly, both at home and in their careers, find themselves suddenly needing to navigate complex money decisions. If you're facing separation, or even just thinking about what it could mean, you are not alone. Your financial wellbeing matters, and the choices you make now can shape your future for decades to come. Here are five critical mistakes women often make during divorce; and how you can avoid them: 1. Shrinking Your Own Success It's common to downplay your achievements or financial independence to keep the peace in a relationship. But making yourself smaller, whether that's declining promotions or avoiding celebrations, can damage your confidence and long-term security. REAL-LIFE EXAMPLE Amanda, 54, felt guilty for out-earning her husband after a major promotion. She stopped talking about work, turned down travel, and apologised for her success. When her marriage ended, she realised she'd lost not just her partner but her own sense of pride. How to avoid this mistake: Own your achievements, celebrate your growth. Your financial independence is a strength, not a liability. Communicate openly, talk about money and success before resentment can build. Seek advice, professional support can help you balance ambition with family harmony. 2. Avoiding Difficult Money Conversations Many couples never discuss the impact of financial changes, like a new job, inheritance, or redundancy, until tension explodes. excerpt: Australia has no inheritance tax, but your family could still face a tax bill. What really happens when assets are passed on.
content: ← Back to Inheritance ARTICLE Inheritance Planning in Australia: What Tax Your Family Really Pays By Andrew Beks Inheritance planning in Australia can be confusing, especially when you assume there's no inheritance tax. While it's true that Australia doesn't have a specific inheritance tax, that doesn't mean your family won't face tax bills down the line. How much tax your loved ones pay on what you leave them often depends on the records you keep today. If you want to protect your family's financial wellbeing, you need to understand what really happens when assets like shares, investment properties, or even the family home are passed on. No Inheritance Tax; But Watch Out for Capital Gains When you pass on shares or investment properties, your children inherit them directly. There's no tax at the point of inheritance. The catch comes later: when your family sells those assets, the taxman takes a slice based on the original purchase price, not the value at the time you passed away. If you bought shares or property decades ago, and your records are missing or incomplete, your family might end up paying far more tax than necessary. The paperwork you leave behind could mean thousands of dollars saved; or lost. Why Good Records Matter for Inheritance Planning Many people don't realise how vital detailed records are. For shares, your loved ones need to know the original purchase price, dates of any additional purchases, and records of dividend reinvestments. For investment properties, it's about purchase contracts, renovation receipts, and costs of capital improvements. Without these, they can't prove what was spent, and the tax bill can soar. REAL-LIFE EXAMPLE Lisa, 57, inherited her father's investment property and a bundle of share certificates. There were no records of what he'd paid, or even when he'd bought them. When she sold the assets, her accountant had to estimate the cost base conservatively, pushing her capital gains tax much higher than it should have been.

content: ARTICLE How Much Risk Can You Really Handle? By Vanessa Stoykov Investors are often asked whether they are conservative, balanced or growth-focused. The label can make risk sound like a fixed personality trait. In reality, risk has several dimensions: how much loss you can financially afford, how much volatility you can emotionally tolerate and how much time the money has to recover. This is where investing becomes less about finding a fashionable answer and more about making a decision that fits an actual human life. Risk is easy to accept in a questionnaire and much harder to live with when the balance falls. The numbers matter, but so do your obligations, confidence, time frame and ability to stay with the decision when life becomes complicated. Capacity and tolerance are different A person with a long time frame may have financial capacity for market risk but still panic during falls. Another may feel emotionally comfortable with risk but need the money too soon to accept it. A strategy must respect both realities rather than treating confidence as capacity. BREAKOUT BOX 1 — THE SIMPLE EXPLANATION Risk capacity is financial. Risk tolerance is emotional. Time frame affects the ability to recover. A suitable plan must consider all three. Would you continue contributing, hold, sell or lose sleep? Your answer is not a moral test. It is information that should shape the plan. There is also an emotional layer that is easy to overlook. title: Investing Isn't Just for Wealthy People
author: Vanessa Stoykov
tags: Investing, Beginner Investing, Building Wealth, Financial Confidence, Money Mindset
excerpt: Why investing is not reserved for wealthy people and how starting with a manageable amount can build knowledge, confidence and financial choice.
content: ARTICLE Investing Isn't Just for Wealthy People By Vanessa Stoykov Investing is often presented through images of wealth: large portfolios, expensive property and people who appear to speak a language the rest of us were never taught. It is easy to believe investing begins only after you have become financially successful. For most people, the opposite is true. Investing is one of the tools ordinary people can use to build greater choice gradually. This is where investing becomes less about finding a fashionable answer and more about making a decision that fits an actual human life. Waiting until you feel wealthy enough to invest can mean missing the one advantage money cannot buy back: time. The numbers matter, but so do your obligations, confidence, time frame and ability to stay with the decision when life becomes complicated. Start with the foundations Before investing, look at urgent bills, expensive debt and whether you have accessible emergency savings. Money needed next month has a different job from money you can leave invested for years. Building a basic buffer reduces the chance that an unexpected expense will force you to sell at a bad time or return to high-cost debt. content: ARTICLE Property or Shares: Which Investment Is Right for Your Life? By Vanessa Stoykov Property and shares are often discussed like rival teams. One person points to borrowing and tangible ownership. Another points to liquidity and diversification. Both can help build wealth, and both can fall in value. The useful question is not which asset wins every argument. It is which characteristics fit your goals, resources and behaviour. It is tangible, but it is not effortless or quickly divisible when you need only part of the money. title: Should You Pay Off Debt or Start Investing?
author: Vanessa Stoykov

content: ARTICLE Should You Pay Off Debt or Start Investing? By Vanessa Stoykov Should extra money reduce debt or go into investments? People often expect one universal mathematical answer. The decision is more personal. A high-interest credit card creates a different equation from a lower-interest long-term loan. Investment returns are uncertain, while reducing debt produces a known saving in interest and can create valuable emotional relief. This is where investing becomes less about finding a fashionable answer and more about making a decision that fits an actual human life. Paying down debt and investing can both strengthen your future. The right order depends on the debt, the risk and your wider financial position. The numbers matter, but so do your obligations, confidence, time frame and ability to stay with the decision when life becomes complicated. Start with costly and dangerous debt High-interest debt can grow faster than a realistic investment return and leave little room for emergencies. Reducing it may be the strongest first priority. Look at the rate, fees and whether the debt is secured against an important asset. Do not allow excitement about investing to distract you from a balance that is compounding against you. BREAKOUT BOX 1 — THE SIMPLE EXPLANATION Debt reduction offers a known interest saving. Investment returns can be positive or negative. Emergency savings help stop debt returning. author: Vanessa Stoykov

content: ARTICLE The Investing Mistakes We Make When Markets Fall By Vanessa Stoykov When markets rise, risk can feel theoretical. When balances fall, the loss feels personal and immediate. Headlines become urgent, confident predictions appear everywhere and doing something feels safer than waiting. This is when long-term plans are often most vulnerable to short-term fear. This is where investing becomes less about finding a fashionable answer and more about making a decision that fits an actual human life. A market fall does not create your investing emotions. Selling to escape the feeling A fall on a statement is painful, but selling turns the current value into an actual exit. Sometimes a sale is appropriate, but panic alone is not a strategy. Ask whether your goal, time frame or circumstances changed, or whether only the price and your emotional state changed. BREAKOUT BOX 1 — THE SIMPLE EXPLANATION Market falls are a normal possibility, not a personal failure. Selling removes exposure to both further falls and potential recovery. Re-entering later requires another difficult decision. An emotional plan is part of an investment plan. content: ARTICLE What Is an ETF? A Simple Explanation for New Investors By Vanessa Stoykov If you have started reading about investing, it probably did not take long before someone mentioned an ETF. ETF stands for exchange-traded fund. While the name sounds technical, the basic concept is straightforward: an ETF can hold a collection of assets, and investors can purchase units in that collection through an exchange. This is where investing becomes less about finding a fashionable answer and more about making a decision that fits an actual human life. ETFs are often described as a simple way to invest, but you should still understand what you own, what it costs and how its value can change. The numbers matter, but so do your obligations, confidence, time frame and ability to stay with the decision when life becomes complicated. Think of an ETF as a basket Depending on the fund, the basket may contain shares in many companies, bonds, property-related investments, commodities or a mix. Some ETFs follow an index representing a market or part of one. You are not buying the index itself; you are buying units in a fund designed to reflect it. BREAKOUT BOX 1 — THE SIMPLE EXPLANATION An ETF is a fund traded on an exchange. It may hold many investments inside one structure. The contents and risk differ from fund to fund. The letters ETF do not guarantee diversification, simplicity or safety. Why people use ETFs ETFs can make diversification more accessible than buying many individual investments separately. title: Stop Saying 'I'm Bad With Money'
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Why turning financial mistakes into an identity makes change harder, and how to build confidence through small evidence.
content: ← Back to Money Mindset ARTICLE Stop Saying 'I'm Bad With Money' By Vanessa Stoykov People say it casually: I'm terrible with numbers. I've always been a spender. My partner handles all that. The sentence may protect you from embarrassment, but it also hands your power away, quietly, every time you repeat it. A missed payment, impulsive purchase or confusing investment does not define your identity. It describes a behaviour or a gap in knowledge. Behaviours and knowledge can change, an identity feels much harder to. Use accurate language Replace 'I'm bad with money' with the specific truth: 'I avoid looking at statements when I feel ashamed.' 'I do not understand my retirement account.' 'I have not learned how to plan irregular expenses.' Specific language may feel less comfortable at first, but it gives you somewhere to begin, which the identity statement never did. Notice, too, how often the phrase gets used to close a conversation rather than open one — it is frequently the last thing said before someone changes the subject, hands the decision to a partner or simply stops paying attention to their own numbers altogether. That closing-down effect is part of why the label is so costly. A vague verdict cannot be worked on. A specific gap can. The moment you swap one for the other, you have already done something a person who is genuinely "bad with money" by nature could not do: you have located the actual problem. It turned out her real issue was a single, very fixable habit: she avoided opening her banking app whenever she felt anxious about her balance, which meant small problems went unnoticed until they became larger ones. title: The Financial Decisions We Make When We're Afraid
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How fear drives avoidance, panic spending, over-control and staying stuck — and a framework for calmer money decisions.
content: ← Back to Money Mindset ARTICLE The Financial Decisions We Make When We're Afraid By Vanessa Stoykov Fear changes our sense of time. A market fall feels permanent. A job problem feels like we will never earn again. A child's distress makes immediate financial rescue feel like the only loving response available in the moment. Under pressure, we may sell, borrow, spend, hide or freeze. Later, when the fear has eased, the decision can look very different from how it felt at the time it was made. Name the emotion and the threat Ask: what exactly am I afraid will happen? Be specific. Losing status is different from losing housing. Disappointing a child is different from being unable to buy food, and confusing the two leads to disproportionate responses. This is not about dismissing emotion. It is about separating the real threat from every imagined consequence that fear has attached to it along the way. Fear rarely arrives with a single, clean prediction — it tends to bring an entire chain of catastrophes, each one less likely than the last, and the further down that chain you go, the less it has to do with the actual decision in front of you. Writing the chain down, rather than letting it run silently in your head, is often enough to break its momentum. Most people find that somewhere around the third or fourth "and then what happens" question, the scenario has drifted a long way from anything grounded in fact. A conversation with his adviser slowed him down long enough to ask a simple question: had his actual retirement date or spending needs changed? They hadn't. title: Three Ways to Improve Your Money Mindset
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Money shapes how we see ourselves as much as what we own. Three practical shifts to build a healthier relationship with money.
content: ← Back to Money Mindset ARTICLE Three Ways to Improve Your Money Mindset By Vanessa Stoykov Money had fascinated me for as long as I can remember. Not necessarily the accumulation and growing of it. More, the impact it has on who we are, how we feel about ourselves and how others view us. Money and self worth are as closely linked as our parental influences. Money pervades every part of our life, determining our opportunities when born, the set of challenges we face, and choices we are able to make in the future. The Western world would tell us that anybody has the opportunity to create abundance. The rags to riches stories are our favourite, and in a democracy, everybody gets a chance to participate if they choose, right? Except that belief is only half true. The playing field has not been evenly stacked, and those with access to money can make better choices. I'm not the first to point this out – there has been so much change, so quickly. We are scared, uncertain and know each of us has to protect our own patch, our own families and communities. This responsibility can be debilitating, especially when access to resources is limited. Why are so many of us are falling into stress traps. Rising rents, rising interest rates, the cost of living soaring, has had a big impact on our quality of life. The stress, anxiety and fear, and the resultant anger has families hurting and people in despair. It also means people that have long had disposable income and the choices that come from that, are no longer able to live life that way. Owning a media business over COVID was not a financial goldmine. I have learned the hard way about budgeting, and curtailing lifestyle choices. And I can say firsthand, it is much harder to find amusement and pleasure alone or with family without spending money. Especially when you are used to having some choices. title: What Does 'Enough' Actually Look Like for You?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How defining enough can bring clarity to saving, spending, work and the kind of life you are trying to fund.
content: ← Back to Money Mindset ARTICLE What Does 'Enough' Actually Look Like for You? By Vanessa Stoykov More is easy to measure. A higher income, larger home, bigger balance or better title gives us a visible score. Enough is harder because it asks us to decide what the score is actually for in the first place. Without that decision, financial life can become endless accumulation or endless anxiety. You may keep sacrificing time and relationships for a finish line that moves every time you approach it, never quite arriving. Enough is personal and seasonal Enough in your 30s may be stability and a deposit. In your 50s it may be flexibility, meaningful work and confidence about housing. After loss or illness, it may simply be time. Do not borrow another person's definition. Social media is very good at showing you what more looks like and very poor at showing the private cost that came with it. It is also worth noticing how quickly a definition of enough can shift once you actually reach it. Many people find that hitting a long-held target doesn't produce the settled feeling they expected — the goalposts simply move, quietly, before they've had time to register the win. Naming that pattern in advance can make it easier to actually pause and notice progress when it arrives, rather than letting it slide straight past. IN PRACTICE A successful surgeon in his early sixties, financially secure many times over by any objective measure, realised during a health scare that he had never actually defined what "enough" meant to him — he had simply kept working towards a bigger number without ever checking whether he'd already passed it. Once he sat down and put real figures against the life he actually wanted — modest travel, time with grandchildren, a paid-off home — he discovered he'd been financially "there" for almost a decade. title: Why Earning More Doesn't Always Make You Feel Financially Secure
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Why financial anxiety can remain after income grows, and how to build security through clarity, systems and enough.
content: ← Back to Money Mindset ARTICLE Why Earning More Doesn't Always Make You Feel Financially Secure By Vanessa Stoykov People often imagine a salary figure at which money anxiety will disappear. They reach it, adjust their life and discover that the worry has simply moved to a larger number, following them upward like a shadow rather than staying behind. This does not mean income is irrelevant. More money can relieve real pressure. But security is a combination of resources, predictability, control and belief. If spending rises with income or fear remains unexamined, the feeling of enough stays permanently out of reach. Lifestyle can absorb every increase A higher income often brings a more expensive home, school, car, holiday or social expectation. Fixed costs grow, and the new salary becomes necessary rather than liberating, often within a surprisingly short window. Before allocating the next increase, decide how much will strengthen savings, debt reduction or investment. Give future security a share before present life expands around the whole amount. A simple rule many people find useful is deciding the split before the money arrives, not after. If half of every future pay rise is automatically redirected towards savings or debt before it ever reaches everyday spending, lifestyle creep has far less room to operate — the decision is made once, calmly, rather than repeatedly under the pull of a slightly larger number landing in the account each month. IN PRACTICE A couple who doubled their combined income over five years, moving into increasingly senior roles, were baffled to find they felt more financially stressed than they had a decade earlier on a much smaller combined salary. title: Your Money Habits Didn't Start With You
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How childhood, family messages and early experiences shape adult money behaviour — and how to choose new patterns.
content: ← Back to Money Mindset ARTICLE Your Money Habits Didn't Start With You By Vanessa Stoykov Long before we earn a salary, we are watching money. We notice whether bills create tension, whether wealthy people are admired or distrusted, whether asking is safe and whether there is ever enough. Children absorb far more about money from atmosphere than from anything they're actually taught. These observations become rules: money disappears, debt is normal, talking about money is rude, success makes people dislike you, a good parent always says yes. We may carry those rules for decades without realising they were learned rather than chosen. Find the original story Think about your earliest money memory and the phrases repeated in your home. Who controlled money? Who worried? What happened when someone wanted more than the family could afford, and how was that handled? The purpose is not to blame parents. They inherited stories too and responded to their own circumstances. The purpose is to see the pattern clearly enough to decide whether it still serves you today. It can help to ask the same questions of a sibling, if you have one, since two children raised in the same house often absorb quite different lessons from it. One might take away that money is dangerous and unpredictable; the other might take away that it always sorts itself out. Comparing notes is often the fastest way to see that the rule you're carrying was never a universal truth — it was one interpretation among several, formed in a particular moment for particular reasons. IN PRACTICE A successful business owner, earning well into six figures, still felt a jolt of panic every time she checked her bank balance — a reaction that made no logical sense given her actual financial position. Tracing it back, she realised it echoed watching her mother anxiously recalculate the grocery budget every single week during a childhood marked by real scarcity. title: Are You Buying a Home — or Buying the Life You Think You Should Have?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How to separate the emotional meaning of property from the home and financial commitment that genuinely suit your life.
content: ← Back to Property ARTICLE Are You Buying a Home — or Buying the Life You Think You Should Have? By Vanessa Stoykov Property is one of the most emotional purchases we make. We are not simply buying walls and land. We may be buying proof that we have succeeded, a childhood dream, a postcode that signals belonging or the life we think our family should have — and it is remarkably easy to mistake that emotional pull for a purely practical decision. That emotional pull is powerful. It can also persuade us to stretch further, commute longer or carry more pressure than our real life can comfortably absorb, especially when the property in question feels like a symbol of arrival rather than simply a place to live. Separate the home from the story Before falling in love with a property, ask what problem you are trying to solve. Do you need stability, more space, proximity to family, a better commute or permission to feel successful? Some of those needs require property. Others may be met in far less expensive ways than a mortgage that stretches for thirty years. Be honest about whose expectations are driving the decision. A home that impresses other people but leaves you anxious every month is an expensive stage set, and the audience for it is usually smaller and less invested than we imagine. IN PRACTICE A couple stretched their budget to buy in a suburb their friends and siblings had all moved to, partly because it felt like proof they'd "made it." Within two years, the extra hour of daily commuting and the tight monthly budget had eroded far more of their quality of life than the postcode had added. When they eventually moved somewhere less impressive but genuinely comfortable, they described it as the first time in years they'd stopped feeling like they were performing for an audience. author: Vanessa Stoykov

content: ← Back to Property ARTICLE Before You Buy Property With Someone, Have These Five Conversations By Vanessa Stoykov Couples, siblings, friends and parents with adult children are increasingly considering property together. Pooling resources can improve a deposit and borrowing capacity, but enthusiasm about the opportunity often races ahead of the difficult questions that determine whether the arrangement actually works long term. A shared address does not guarantee shared assumptions. Before signing anything, talk through ownership, money, use, change and exit — five conversations that are far easier to have before there's a property, and much harder once there is. One: what does each person own? Discuss the ownership structure and whether shares reflect deposits, repayments or another agreement. Legal ownership, beneficial expectations and casual promises should not be left to memory, no matter how close the relationship currently feels. Get legal advice on the structure and record the agreement properly. Different arrangements can have different tax, estate and legal effects that aren't obvious until they matter. This is worth doing even when the co-buyers are family, and arguably more so. Close relationships can make people reluctant to raise questions that feel like they imply distrust, which is precisely how casual verbal understandings end up standing in for proper agreements. A document does not weaken the relationship; it simply removes the need for anyone's memory to be the final word later on. IN PRACTICE Two sisters bought an investment property together, splitting the deposit 60/40 based on their savings but never formally documenting it — assuming their closeness made paperwork unnecessary. Years later, when one sister wanted to sell to fund a business and the other didn't, they discovered they had no written agreement about buyout terms, valuation methods or timelines. title: Should I Stay or Should I Sell? The Property Decision That Gets Harder in Your 50s
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How to think through selling, staying or downsizing in midlife when money, identity, family and future needs collide.
content: ← Back to Property ARTICLE Should I Stay or Should I Sell? The Property Decision That Gets Harder in Your 50s By Vanessa Stoykov In midlife, property decisions carry history. The family home may represent children growing up, a marriage, years of renovations and the neighbourhood that knows you. It may also carry a large mortgage, rising maintenance and rooms no longer used — sometimes both of those things sitting inside the same set of walls at once. That is why 'just downsize' can feel glib. You are not only comparing sale prices. You are considering identity, community, security and the shape of the next chapter, and none of those weigh as neatly as a bank valuation does. Start with the future, not the floor plan Imagine ordinary life five and ten years from now. How much space will you use? Where will family live? How important are transport, stairs, health services and a support network? Would a move free time and money, or take you away from what makes life work day to day? A smaller home is not automatically cheaper once transaction costs, strata fees, renovations and location are considered. Use realistic figures rather than assumptions inherited from a friend's very different experience. IN PRACTICE One widow held onto her four-bedroom family home for nearly a decade after her children moved out, convinced downsizing meant giving something up. When she finally sold and moved into a smaller two-bedroom apartment closer to her sister, she was surprised to find the grief she'd anticipated never really arrived — what she felt instead was relief at no longer maintaining rooms she hadn't entered in years, and the extra cash freed up a level of financial breathing room she hadn't had in a long time. Measure pressure as well as equity A valuable home can make you look wealthy while leaving very little cash flow. title: The Bank of Mum and Dad: Help or Financial Headache?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: What families should discuss before parents provide a deposit, loan, gift or guarantee for an adult child's property.
content: ← Back to Property ARTICLE The Bank of Mum and Dad: Help or Financial Headache? By Vanessa Stoykov For many young adults, family help feels like the only bridge into property. Parents want to help and may feel proud that years of work can give their child a start. The conversation often begins emotionally: 'We'll find a way.' What follows that sentence, though, is rarely as simple as the sentiment behind it. But a gift, loan or guarantee is not one simple act. It can affect borrowing capacity, retirement security, siblings, future partners and what happens if the child cannot repay — consequences that often only become visible years after the initial, well-meaning conversation. Know which kind of help you are offering A gift, a family loan, co-ownership and a guarantee create very different risks. Families sometimes use the words interchangeably and discover later that each person understood the arrangement differently — sometimes only when a relationship breaks down or a repayment is missed. Put the terms in writing with proper advice. Clarify ownership, repayments, interest, time frames and what happens after separation, illness, job loss or sale. An awkward conversation now is far easier than a family dispute later, even though it rarely feels that way in the moment. IN PRACTICE A retired couple guaranteed part of their son's mortgage so he could buy his first home, assuming the arrangement was a formality that would never actually come into play. When his relationship ended two years later and he fell behind on repayments during the settlement, the bank came directly to them. They hadn't understood that a guarantee could put their own home at risk — they'd thought of it as simply "vouching" for him, not as a debt they could personally end up owing. title: Why Property FOMO Can Be an Expensive Emotion
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: How fear of missing out can distort property decisions, increase financial pressure and make buyers ignore their real priorities.
content: ← Back to Property ARTICLE Why Property FOMO Can Be an Expensive Emotion By Vanessa Stoykov Property fear of missing out has a particular intensity. Prices rise, friends buy, auctions move quickly and every delay feels like permanent failure. The mind jumps from 'I have not bought yet' to 'I will never be able to buy,' and that leap happens far faster than the actual market usually moves. Under that pressure, people stop evaluating a property and start trying to escape a feeling. That is when compromises multiply and limits begin to move, often without the buyer even noticing how far they've shifted from where they started. Urgency narrows your vision FOMO encourages buyers to treat all action as progress. They overlook building issues, accept unsuitable locations, waive sensible checks or borrow to the edge of their capacity because doing nothing feels unbearable in the moment. The danger is not only overpaying. It is spending years servicing a decision that never matched the life you wanted, made in a headspace that had very little to do with the actual property in front of you. IN PRACTICE After watching three auctions go well above their budget, one couple finally "won" a fourth by bidding $60,000 over their original limit — relief flooding in the moment the hammer fell. It was only weeks later, once the adrenaline wore off, that they properly registered the commute, the renovation costs they'd skipped assessing, and the repayment figure they'd agreed to under pressure. They later said the auction room had felt more like a competition to win than a decision about where they'd actually live. It's about trust, respect, and the future you're building together. Financial planning after 50 is rarely straightforward, but open conversations are crucial. 1. Ignoring the Importance of Financial Transparency One of the most common mistakes in second marriages is assuming that what's “yours” and “mine” doesn't need to be discussed. In reality, large financial decisions, especially those affecting family stability, should always be shared. Secrecy can erode trust and leave you questioning what else is hidden. It's easy to think that using personal savings means you don't need to consult your spouse. But for many, the issue is not just the money, but the lack of honesty and partnership. title: Could You Afford to Leave Your Relationship?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: Why everyone should understand their independent financial position, even in a happy relationship.
content: ← Back to Relationships ARTICLE Could You Afford to Leave Your Relationship? By Vanessa Stoykov There is a question many people do not want to ask: if this relationship ended, could I support myself? It can sound disloyal when things are happy. But understanding your financial position is not an exit strategy. It is basic awareness, the kind most of us would want any adult in our life to have regardless of how content they currently are. For someone who has spent years out of the workforce, worked part-time or allowed one person to manage every account, the answer may be confronting. Housing, legal costs, childcare and two households can turn an emotional decision into a financial emergency almost overnight. Dependence can happen slowly One partner takes parental leave. The family moves for the other person's career. One becomes better at managing bills. Passwords, documents and investment decisions gradually sit with them. Years later, the other partner may not know what the household owns or owes, without either person ever consciously choosing that outcome. This can happen in loving relationships. It can also become control. If you are prevented from accessing money, punished for spending or frightened to ask questions, consider confidential specialist support — the line between "he handles the finances" and coercive control is not always obvious from the inside. IN PRACTICE After fifteen years as a stay-at-home parent, one woman realised during a routine conversation with a friend that she genuinely did not know which bank her family used, whether they had any savings, or what their mortgage balance was. Nothing about her marriage was in crisis — she simply had never needed to ask, and her husband had never thought to tell her. title: Financial Infidelity: What Happens When Your Partner Is Hiding Money From You?
author: Vanessa Stoykov
excerpt: What financial infidelity looks like, why people hide debt or spending, and how couples can respond to the breach of trust.
content: ← Back to Relationships ARTICLE Financial Infidelity: What Happens When Your Partner Is Hiding Money From You? By Vanessa Stoykov A credit card statement arrives unexpectedly. A loan application reveals a debt you knew nothing about. You discover an account, a pattern of spending or a major purchase that has been deliberately hidden. The amount matters, but the first feeling is often betrayal — the sense that the relationship you thought you were in wasn't entirely the one you were actually living in. Financial infidelity can include secret debt, undisclosed accounts, gambling, hidden savings, lies about income or disguised purchases. The behaviour varies, but the defining issue is that one person knowingly withheld information that affects the other, often for months or years before it surfaces. Why people hide money Some people fear conflict or judgement. Some feel controlled and create a private account as their only sense of independence. Others are ashamed of debt, compulsive spending or a decision that has grown beyond them. Sometimes secrecy is used deliberately to hold power or prepare to leave, which is a very different situation from shame-driven concealment. Understanding the reason can explain the behaviour, but it does not erase its impact. Compassion and accountability can exist at the same time, and neither one cancels out the need for the other. IN PRACTICE One man discovered, after ten years of marriage, that his wife had been quietly paying down her sister's debts for years using a credit card he didn't know existed. She hadn't spent the money on herself — she'd been trying to help family without triggering what she assumed would be his disapproval. The debt itself was manageable once it was out in the open. What took longer to repair was the fact that she'd decided, alone, that he couldn't be trusted with the truth. content: ← Back to Relationships ARTICLE Should You Combine Finances After 50? Financial Planning for New Relationships By Vanessa Stoykov Falling in love again after 50 can feel like a second chance at happiness; but when you've rebuilt your life after divorce, combining finances with a new partner raises big questions. Financial planning after 50 isn't just about numbers, it's about your sense of safety, trust, and the future you want to build. It's common to wonder: Is keeping assets separate a sign of mistrust? Are you letting your past dictate your future, or simply protecting hard-won independence? If you're facing these questions, you're not alone. 1. Understand What Your Money Means to You Money is rarely just about dollars. Your home and savings often represent security, resilience, and freedom, especially if you've survived a difficult divorce or financial setback. It's natural to want to protect what you've rebuilt, even when you're excited about a new relationship. Before you make any decisions, take time to reflect on what your assets truly mean to you; and why. This isn't about being selfish; it's about honouring your journey so far. 2. Don't Let Pressure or Guilt Make the Decision New relationships can bring pressure from all sides, partners, children, even friends. You might hear that combining everything is 'the natural next step,' or be told that wanting to keep something separate means you don't trust your partner. content: ← Back to Relationships ARTICLE The Money Conversation Every Couple Should Have Before Things Go Wrong By Vanessa Stoykov Most couples know what they are doing this weekend. Far fewer could clearly explain the full state of their shared finances. They may know the mortgage payment or the approximate savings balance, but not every debt, insurance policy, beneficiary, account or financial obligation. Life carries on, one person takes responsibility for the admin, and the conversation is postponed indefinitely because there never seems to be an urgent reason to have it. Then something happens. A job disappears. A parent needs care. Someone becomes unwell. A relationship ends. Suddenly the person who was not involved has to make major decisions with incomplete information and very little time, often while also managing the emotional weight of whatever triggered the crisis in the first place. Knowing is not the same as controlling Some people resist financial conversations because they fear being judged or losing independence. Others assume that because their partner handles the money, everything must be fine. But shared visibility is not about asking permission for every coffee. It is about both adults understanding the commitments that shape their lives together. Each person should know where important documents are kept, what is owed, what is owned and what would happen if either person could not work or manage the household finances. If that feels uncomfortable, it is a sign the conversation matters, not a reason to avoid it. content: ← Back to Relationships ARTICLE When One Person Earns More: How Money Changes the Power in a Relationship By Vanessa Stoykov When one person earns significantly more, money can quietly alter the balance of a relationship. It may begin with practical choices about who pays for what. Over time, the higher earner can start to feel entitled to the final say, while the lower earner feels they must justify ordinary spending — sometimes without either person consciously deciding that this is how things should work. Sometimes nobody names the change. You hear it in comments such as, 'I'm the one paying for it' or 'I need to ask before I buy anything.' At that point the problem is no longer only income. It is power, and power that goes unspoken tends to grow rather than settle on its own. Income is not the only contribution A household is held together by far more than paid work. Caring for children, running family logistics, supporting a partner's career and managing a home all have value. One person may earn less because the couple jointly decided that another priority mattered more for a period — a decision that was shared, even if the income gap now looks one-sided. If only salary is recognised, the lower earner can become financially vulnerable and emotionally diminished. Both people need language that acknowledges the complete contribution each is making, not just the one that shows up as a number on a payslip. content: ← Back to Relationships ARTICLE Why Smart Couples Still Fight About Money By Vanessa Stoykov Two intelligent, capable people can build successful careers, raise a family and manage a complicated life together, yet still have the same argument about money for years. One thinks the other spends too freely. The other feels watched and judged. One wants every dollar accounted for. The other wants to enjoy life now. Neither person is necessarily irresponsible, but both can leave the conversation feeling misunderstood. That is because money is rarely just a number inside a relationship. It can represent safety, independence, love, power, status, generosity or fear. When couples fight about a purchase, a budget or a bank balance, they are often arguing about what that money means to them rather than the transaction itself. The number on the receipt is almost never the real subject of the fight. You are bringing two money histories together We learn about money long before we earn it. One person may have grown up in a home where money was tight and every bill caused stress. Their partner may have grown up believing there would always be enough. One learned that saving is protection. The other learned that spending is how you celebrate, connect or show love. These early lessons become automatic. The saver may see a spontaneous holiday as dangerous. The spender may see refusing it as joyless or controlling. If neither person explains the history underneath their reaction, each can assume the worst about the other. content: ← Back to Retirement ARTICLE Retirement Planning Australia: How to Design a Purposeful Next Chapter By Vanessa Stoykov Retirement planning in Australia has changed dramatically. Retirement isn't just a financial event, it's a whole life transition, and for many, it brings up big questions about identity, purpose, and connection. Recent research from UniSuper's Retire with Purpose Report 2025 highlights that most people don't feel completely comfortable as they enter retirement. Money creates opportunity, but it doesn't automatically create a good life in retirement. 1. Get Clear on Your Financial Position The foundation of any confident retirement plan is clarity. Knowing what you have, what you'll need, and how long your resources might last is crucial. Many people underestimate their lifespan or overestimate what their superannuation will provide. Confidence in your numbers helps you make better life decisions. Gather all your super balances and pension statements. Plan for Social Connection and Contribution Retirement isn't all about money. The loss of structure and daily interaction can leave many people feeling isolated. Balancing the desire for security with the need to enjoy life while you're healthy enough to do it. Remember: retirement is a life decision, not just a financial one. If you're struggling to enjoy your hard-earned savings, you're not failing, you're facing a very real emotional hurdle shared by many. The home you've worked so hard for should provide you with peace of mind, not just a legacy for your children. 2.
